title: HTTP Fundamentals and Methods
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of http fundamentals and methods.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: HTTP is a widely used application-layer protocol for exchanging requests and responses on the web. A request includes a method and target; responses include status codes. Common methods include GET for retrieval, POST for submitting or creating, PUT for replacing, PATCH for partial updates, and DELETE for removal. Method semantics matter; exact behavior depends on the API.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing basic HTTP vocabulary helps use web APIs correctly and understand request behavior.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
HTTP is a widely used application-layer protocol for exchanging requests and responses on the web. A request includes a method and target; responses include status codes. Common methods include GET for retrieval, POST for submitting or creating, PUT for replacing, PATCH for partial updates, and DELETE for removal. Method semantics matter; exact behavior depends on the API.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

examples.title: Choose a retrieval method
examples.explanation: GET is commonly used to retrieve a representation.

examples.title: Submit data
examples.explanation: POST commonly submits data or requests an operation.

examples.title: Replace resource concept
examples.explanation: PUT is commonly used to replace or create a resource at a known target.

examples.title: Partial update concept
examples.explanation: PATCH commonly applies a partial update.

examples.title: Request deletion
examples.explanation: DELETE commonly requests removal of a resource.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: For a fictional library API, match operations (list books, create book, replace book, update one field, delete book) to HTTP methods. Explain your choices.
steps: For a fictional library API, match operations (list books, create book, replace book, update one field, delete book) to HTTP methods. Explain your choices.
Sketch the communication sequence and identify the client/server roles.
Define expected success and failure outcomes.
Choose checks, timeout or retry behavior where appropriate.
Review your design for privacy and safe handling.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Design method choices for an API with courses, lessons, and learner bookmarks. For each method, state the intended effect and whether repeating the request should generally be safe.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy service; do not include live secrets.
Design method choices for an API with courses, lessons, and learner bookmarks. For each method, state the intended effect and whether repeating the request should generally be safe.
Document assumptions, edge cases, and how you would test them.

hints: PATCH generally changes part of a representation.
DELETE requests removal; check the service's documented behavior.
